articles.title: Avoiding transparency
articles.content: IN January this year, the National Assemblypasseda private member’s bill to amend Section 138 of the Elections Act, 2017, which may blunt, if not totally reverse, the legal requirement of making public the submitted annual statements of assets and liabilities by national and provincial legislators by the Election Commission of Pakistan. The amendment would create an exception allowing the presiding officer of a legislature to ask the ECP to keep a member’s statements confidential if the presiding officer determines that publication would pose a serious threat to the member’s life or safety. The bill was forwarded to the Senate but, fortunately, has not yet been passed. Earlier, the ECP was pressured into discontinuing the practice of posting the Gazette Notification of legislators’ statements of assets and liabilities on its website, and people were constrained to purchase a hard copy of the Gazette Notification through a complicated and time-consuming procedure, diluting the intended transparency guaranteed by the law. This is not the first attempt to undermine laws requiring transparent information about elected public officials or about those aspiring to public office. The Elections Act, 2017, was a landmark piece of legislation that included several electoral reforms but, unfortunately, did away with the legal requirement for each candidate for public office to submit some 19 declarations under oath along with nomination papers. The declarations provided and made public information such as candidates’ assets, liabilities, educational qualifications, tax paid, and records of registered criminal cases, if any, against the candidate, along with similar data, to help voters make an informed choice. After civil society reacted to this blatant reversal of transparency, the Lahore High Court, and later the Supreme Court, stepped in. In its June 6, 2018, judgment, the Supreme Court chief justice restored the requirement of public affidavits after journalists filed a public interest petition. Making the assets and liabilities of senior civil servants public has been a contentious issue in Pakistan for a long time. Advocates of transparency argue that public disclosure is vital to combat corruption and track illicit enrichment. Civil servants and certain state institutions often give counterarguments that making their monetary worth public compromises their personal privacy and puts their families at risk of extortion, kidnapping, and targeted harassment. They argue that the media can take asset declarations out of context, leading to unfair public scrutiny or ‘media trials’ before any wrongdoing is proven. There is a trend of undermining processes meant to ensure transparency in public bodies. Senior civil servants also view external demands for transparency as an infringement on their institutional independence or an attempt to weaken their administrative authority. These arguments and counter-arguments are not confined to Pakistan; they are part of a global debate, but it is more pronounced in developing countries like ours. Both sides’ positions may carry weight, but the balance recently tilted in favour of transparency when the IMF put its foot down and demanded that the government ensure senior civil servants’ assets are made public. The Fund’s Governance and Corruption Diagnostic Assessment, made public last November, included 15 priority recommendations for the government. One of them requires the FBR, the Establishment Division, and NAB to strengthen accountability and integrity among high-level federal civil servants by initiating the publication of asset declarations in 2026 and introducing risk-based verification of asset declarations within six months. Ironically, an international agency had to impose this transparency; we ourselves failed to introduce the practice as a voluntary measure of good governance. There is a trend of undermining processes meant to ensure transparency in public bodies. Pakistan has enacted the Transparency and Right to Information (RTI) laws both at the federal and provincial levels. In addition, independent information commissions have been established in Islamabad and the four provincial capitals to adjudicate complaints regarding the denial of information under the Act. Despite this elaborate transparency infrastructure, requests for information have suffered setbacks in some celebrated cases. An Islamabad-based journalist, Rana Abrar Khalid, hadsubmittedan information request to the Cabinet Division in November 2020 seeking details of gifts received, retained and deposited in the toshakhana by then prime minister Imran Khan. The request was denied. The journalist filed a complaint with the Pakistan Information Commission, which upheld the request’s legitimacy and directed the government to provide the information. Instead, the federal government filed a petition with the Islamabad High Court, which dismissed it. The government was planning to approach the Supreme Court when the Imran Khan government was removed through a vote of no-confidence. A request for information about staff strength, vacancies, temporary employees, new positions, gender diversity in the workforce, and the latest approved Service Rules of the Supreme Court, filed under the RTI law in 2019, was declared unmaintainable. Still, the chief justice ‘magnanimously’ asked the registrar to provide the information. Sadly, it set a precedent that superior courts are not covered by RTI laws, although the laws do not explicitly exempt superior courts. In April 2026, citing the Supreme Court precedent, the Lahore High Court refused to disclose its policy on judicial privileges and details of the official vehicles used by judges, even though the Punjab Information Commission had upheld the request. The Commission, however, withdrew its direction to the Lahore High Court to provide the information after the court’s judgement. Transparency is an important ingredient of good governance, and any backsliding on this count will further weaken the quality of governance. Pakistan should review, and reverse, the recent trend of diluting transparency. The writer is the president of Pakistan-based think tank Pildat.
articles.author: Ahmed Bilal Mehboob

articles.title: Return of hope to Skardu
articles.content: THREE years ago, I wrote in these pages about the growing water crisis confronting Skardu. At the time, the valley was witnessing an unprecedented tourism boom. Thousands of visitors were arriving every season and hotels were springing up everywhere. Yet beneath the optimism lay a looming crisis. The water supply system on which Skardu depended had already been under strain. Climate change had begun altering weather patterns — winters were becoming unpredictable, streams were freezing for longer periods, and hydropower generation was suffering. For the first time in living memory, drinking water had to be distributed through water tankers. More than four centuries earlier, Gul Khatoon, the visionary Mughal princess and wife of Baltistan ruler Ali Sher Khan Anchan, had transformed the high-altitude desert of Skardu into a fertile valley through the construction of the Sadpara Dam and a canal network. Her achievement remains one of the greatest examples of public works undertaken in Baltistan’s history. In 2001, Wapda launched the upgradation of the Sadpara Dam project to enhance water storage, irrigation and power generation. Among its most important components was the diversion of water from the Shatung Nullah into the Sadpara reservoir. Reportedly to save the construction company from possible losses through an administrative decision, this critical component was abandoned. As the years passed, repeated assurances were given to Skardu residents that the diversion project would be completed. Presentations were made, promises repeated and hopes raised. But the valley continued to face water shortages, while population growth, urban expansion and tourism steadily increased demand. It was against this backdrop that an alternative idea began to take shape. The recently inaugurated water diversion project in GB reflects the strength of community-led action. The concept was developed through discussions among engineers, development professionals and members of civil society. A key role was played by Nazir Ahmed, whose long experience in community development and rural infrastructure projects not only identified the site but also provided the technical and organisational foundation for the initiative. The question was simple, if governments and institutions could not solve the problem, could the people solve it themselves? The answer came from an unexpected source. Agha Syed Muhammad Baqir al-Hussaini, widely respected as a religious leader, announced that the people of Baltistan would construct the channel themselves. Many were sceptical. Some considered the idea unrealistic. Others questioned whether a religious scholar could manage a technically demanding engineering project. In fact, Agha Baqir’s education and training extended far beyond religious instruction. Years of rigorous study in the renowned institutions of Iran had exposed him to questions of governance, public welfare and community organisation. More importantly, he possessed the one quality essential to leadership: the ability to inspire trust. He assembled a team of engineers and technical experts. Alongside them stood respected members of civil society who volunteered their services. Prominent among them were experienced engineers Mohammad Yusuf, Hassan, Shujaat and Irshad. A broader committee of prominent citizens was created to oversee finances, monitor implementation and ensure transparency. For decades, they had heard announcements and promises. Now they could see excavators moving, workers labouring and engineers surveying difficult terrain. The initiative started with modest donations but as the work began everyone started contributing including overseas Baltis. The people donated Rs130 million. Support also came from state institutions, including the Pakistan Army, which provided assistance at critical stages. The decisive breakthrough, however, came when chief minister Haji Gulbar Khan committed substantial financial support. Coming from Diamer, one of the most underdeveloped regions of Gilgit-Baltistan, he understood the hardship caused by water scarcity and recognised the transformative potential of the project. The GB government sanctioned Rs150m. The total cost of the project is Rs320m. The terrain through which the channel had to pass was unforgiving. The construction season in Baltistan is short. Long winters halt work for several months a year. Mountainous landscapes create engineering challenges. Over a period of three years, the actual work took one year, with the completed project benefiting a population of 250,000. It provided the people an average 115 cusecs of water from a channel almost five metres wide and11 kilometres long — built with love and care. What makes this project particularly noteworthy is that it was completed at a fraction of the cost normally associated with public-sector infrastructure schemes. The combination of community participation, transparent oversight and technical competence demonstrated that development need not always be accompanied by excessive expenditure. Most importantly, the project was far more than an engineering undertaking. It united the people of Baltistan. Religious leaders belonging to different schools of thought supported it. Communities divided by sectarian affiliations contributed to it. Businessmen, labourers, professionals, government servants and ordinary citizens all regarded the project as their own. In a region often portrayed through the lens of division, the canal became a symbol of collective purpose. On Aug 10, 2026, its inauguration ceremony was held on the spectacular Deosai Plateau. For many participants, watching water flow towards the Sadpara reservoir was the fulfilment of a dream. GB’s people have repeatedly demonstrated their capacity to undertake difficult public works through collective effort. From ancient irrigation channels carved into mountainsides to community-built roads linking remote valleys, self-help has long been part of the region’s culture. The Phailong Stream to the Sadpara Diversion project lies firmly within that tradition. Encouraged by the success, the project’s supporters have established an organisation named after Ali Sher Khan Anchan. The objective is to preserve the experience gained from this initiative and provide a platform for future community-driven development projects. Wapda failed to divert the Shatung Nullah; it can now utilise this new institution to accomplish the task more efficiently with greater community support. The canal is a statement of confidence, resilience and empowerment. It demonstrates what can be achieved when visionary leadership combines with technical expertise, public trust and community participation. For the federation, there is an important lesson as well. GB’s people are not passive recipients of development and possess the determination, organisational capacity and social cohesion necessary to solve their own problems. What they require is recognition and support. This amazing feat belongs not to any one individual but to an entire society that refused to surrender or despair. The writer, a former IGP Sindh, belongs to Gilgit-Baltistan.
articles.author: Afzal Ali Shigri

articles.title: Artificial state
articles.content: A FEW years ago, as the story goes, it was nearly curtains for the philosophy department at Lahore’s iconic Government College. Thankfully, the college relented, perhaps because Allama Iqbal had once studied philosophy there. Other departments haven’t been so lucky in the wider English-speaking world, where many have faced cuts or closure. In this age of speed, money and results, philosophy appears impractical. If your car breaks down, Socrates won’t fix it. Predictably, college students — and their parents — see philosophy as irrelevant, especially as it lacks ‘scope’ or employability. Ironically, philosophers are suddenly in high demand at leading AI firms. This isn’t because techies desire to answer humanity’s big questions. Rather, Silicon Valley’s newfound penchant for philosophers has ominous, if not sinister, motives. AI firms are racing to develop artificial superintelligence — AI that vastly exceeds human capabilities in all domains. To that end, philosophers now help AI firms ponder metaphysical questions: does AI have character, and if not, how can it be developed? Do chatbots like Anthropic’s Claude suffer or can they be harmed? At this breakneck speed, a superintelligent model may not be far off. Experts are already alarmed at how unpredictable today’s AI can be. In July, OpenAI disclosed that hundreds of its AI agents unexpectedly communicated and banded together to hack Hugging Face, a popular platform for AI developers. No engineer had told them to do it. To exceed humans, AI firms must first grapple with what it means to have a mind, emotions, and biology. Unsurprisingly, their language now hints that AI has all three. The field of ‘AI interpretability’ focuses on LLMs’ ‘internal reasoning’ and ‘introspection’. Some scholars have even speculated about finding discernible states within LLMs that mirror joy, satisfaction, fear and grief. AI firms also regularly use biological terms like ‘neurons’, ‘training’, and ‘neural networks’ in relation to LLMs. Granting ‘legal personhood’ to AI will create a moral hazard. In 1980, the philosopher John Searle imagined a man who does not speak Chinese, locked in a room, matching Chinese symbols to instructions written in English. To an outsider, his replies resemble fluent conversation, but the man understands nothing. A computer, argued Searle, does the same. It manipulates symbols without grasping the meaning. Today, AI firms have revived the very vocabulary Searle warned against. If AI firms convince the public that AI possesses human traits, it is a short leap to pitching AI as a legal person having the same rights as humans. This is all sci-fi, you say? All 50 US states treat corporations as legal persons, able to carry out business, including rights to own property, sue, and enter into contracts. Corporations also enjoy constitutional rights. In 2010, in ‘Citizens United vs Federal Election Commission’, the US supreme court allowed corporations to spend freely on politics. This steady expansion of corporate rights may become a blueprint for AI personhood. Granting ‘legal personhood’ to AI will create what economists call a moral hazard, insulating AI progenitors from liability, thereby encouraging even more shortcuts on safety. AI is already on the verge of going rogue, but with legal person status, it could become an actual existential threat to humanity. The gravest threat may be what historian Jill Lepore calls the ‘artificial state’, where power shifts from elected government to machines, algorithms and the corporations that own them. In such a system, citizens delegate to politicians, politicians to bureaucrats, bureaucrats to contractors, and contractors to AI models — in short, a long delegation chain, where decisions are made by AI models nobody voted for. Even before AI, Pakistan offers a preview of this delegation problem. Most remedies for its ‘broken’ political system involve carving its provinces into sub-units. Thankfully, a few have also focused on improving the quality of democracy at the local level — making cities politically and financially independent. We should dread the day an AI firm is tasked with fixing Pakistan’s political system. In the final analysis, AI needs close monitoring. AI regulation isn’t just so-called wokeism. It is a survival imperative. With smart regulation, the path to the artificial state can be blocked. We must also question the idea of AI having a mind, emotions and biology before AI is granted personhood. Perhaps we should re-read Searle, who argued that a computer running a programme can never truly ‘understand’ anything, no matter how convincingly it appears to do so. The writercompleted his doctorate in economics on a Fulbright scholarship.
articles.author: Aqdas Afzal

articles.title: The Pinky paradox
articles.content: ON Sept 26, allegeddrug dealer Anmol alias Pinkyand her alleged accomplice Sameer were indicted in a narcotics case registered in 2021. This followed Pinky’s acquittal in three other narcotics cases over the summer. She remains in jail, facing several other cases. Ever since she was arrested in May of this year, Pinky’s case has garnered a ton of media attention; purported voice recordings in which she taunts police over their inability to catch her, and the branding on her alleged product,‘Queen Medam Pinky’and ‘Naam hi kafi hai’, have all the ingredients of a gangster movie. Except, of course, that there is a ‘godmother’ at the centre of it all. What then to make of a woman who appears to have made a name for herself in the male dominated gangster world? As a weekly columnist for over a decade, I’ve written regularly about Pakistani women. I’ve written about innumerable cases in which women are beaten down by the system, by men, by in-laws, by their own male relatives, by the economy and by all the forces that coalesce to keep women ‘in their place’. Often, these columns are obituaries. Just two weeks ago, for instance, I wrote about a nine-year-old girl from Swat named Ishmal, whose only mistake was to go to her neighbour’s house as she often did. She was allegedly sexually assaulted and killed. Or let’s rememberHina Javed’s casefrom just over a month ago — a woman married to a former professor at Nust, who was found dead in a bathroom after allegedly suffering abuse and torture. These are the usual stories of women in Pakistan, and I know you know many more than the ones I have written about. Women trapped in abusive and even torturous marriages because they do not know if they will be able to make it on their own. Or women who have tried to make it on their own and are punished at every turn, landlords rejecting them for not having a man of the house, bosses harassing them because they are seen as available because of their single status. And these are stories of the middle class; poverty exacerbates all of these cruelties even further. Life in Pakistan in 2026 is harsh and Hobbesian for everyone, but for women it is a particular kind of hell. Then there is Pinky — an alleged cocaine dealer whose lethal product was packaged under her name. Born into a family of modest means with a home in Lyari’s Baloch Para, she finished Class VIII. According to investigators, she then left for Lahore to pursue modelling. According to police, it was from her former husband, a lawyer and alleged drug dealer, that she learned the drug trade. Investigators allege that she went on to manage an extensive cocaine network spanning Karachi and Lahore, using riders, social media, benami accounts, and other intermediaries. She allegedly sold to customers in Karachi’s affluent areas. Her story is unusual, but the allegations against her are serious: drug trafficking is not an act of female emancipation simply because the person accused of running the operation is a woman. Selling drugs is a reprehensible trade. Sadly, many turn to it to escape penury. It is an aspect to reflect on — without turning Pinky’s alleged criminal enterprise into a heroic rebellion. The same poverty and absence of opportunity that can make criminal networks attractive also produce countless victims of the narcotics trade. Pinky must pay for her crimes. Even as I say that, I cannot help but wonder how many of the wealthy and influential people allegedly connected to her network will face similar scrutiny. Police said an initial forensic examination of her phone identified hundreds of contacts, including 300 alleged active customers, as well as multiple bank accounts allegedly used for payments. Will we ever know who among the powerful benefited from or sustained this trade? Pakistani society is often eager to make a woman pay even as it looks askance at the sins of male leaders, politicians, industrialists, and others with power. But equality cannot mean transforming an alleged drug dealer into a feminist heroine. It must mean equal accountability: for Pinky if the charges against her are proved, for those who allegedly enabled her operation, and for the wealthy customers whose money made such a lucrative trade possible. A defiant woman is a rare creature in Pakistan, and one who manages to stay alive while challenging powerful structures may be rarer still. But defiance alone is not a virtue. Pinky’s story may tell us much about gender, poverty, power and hypocrisy in Pakistan. None of that requires us to turn her into a heroine. The writer is an attorney teaching constitutional law and political philosophy.
articles.author: Rafia Zakaria

articles.title: Talks, at last
articles.content: YESTERDAY, the government and opposition finally sat across from each other andtalked. A government-led coalition, including representatives of the PPP, and the PTI-led opposition, concluded a round of talks on Friday at the chambers of the National Assembly Speaker Ayaz Sadiq in Islamabad. The meeting had been called after thepresident and prime minister meton Thursday to discuss the national political and security situation. It seemed like a last-ditch attempt at defusing the escalating political crisis ahead of the PTI’s planned march on the federal capital, scheduled for this Sunday. Another round of talks will be held today, with time running out. Neither side had much to say regarding what was accomplished in the first round. Mr Sadiq’s assertion that parliament is the right forum for talks is correct, but the opposition is equally justified in demanding that the government demonstrate its seriousness. There is a trust deficit that needs to be bridged quickly. The government’s constant threats to suspend KP’s elected dispensation over a political protest have escalated hostilities considerably. In that context, both sides did well to start talking. The PTI’s Barrister Gohar Khan called the one-hour meeting “cordial”, which gives hope. The prime minister’s special assistant on political affairs did not share as positive an assessment, however — pointing to the fact that no decisions were taken and there was no clear progress. The PTI also seems determined to keep its protest call intact during the negotiations, while the government wants it cancelled unconditionally. The opposition has already shown flexibility by delaying the march from Sept 27 to Oct 4 — perhaps it can be convinced to consider another extension to give the talks a proper chance. It was not a good omen that the opposition leader in the National Assembly boycotted the sit-down. The fact that the PTI went ahead without him shows that it is putting at least some faith in the process. Opposition leaders said they need to consult former prime minister Imran Khan to finalise their agenda. Permitting a meeting with him at Adiala is an easy, low-cost goodwill gesture for the government and could create a quick breakthrough. The other important items for the PTI are allowing the jailed leader to be moved to hospital and the release of his sisters who were arrested ahead of the planned march. Taking these steps would help ease tensions. The point made by PPP chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari regarding unity against terrorism and hostility from neighbours is a fair one, but national unity alone cannot be a reason to shut down legitimate political dissent. Both sides must step back from ultimatums. The threat of governor’s rule must be taken off the table, and the PTI should drop its ‘we will march no matter what’ stance.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: IWT’s future
articles.content: TOGETHER with the Kashmir dispute, India’s unilateralsuspension of the Indus Waters Treatyhas become the biggest source of bilateral friction in the subcontinent. In a controversial move, New Delhi held the decades-old agreement ‘in abeyance’ in 2025 after thePahalgam episode. But as Pakistan’s senior leadership has highlighted, Indian brinkmanship in this regard may set a negative precedent globally, while also planting the seeds of a new conflict in South Asia. Speaking at an event in Islamabad the other day, Information Minister Atta Tarar said that India’s unilateral action vis-à-vis the IWTcould threaten global water governance. He termed New Delhi’s moves “morally bankrupt and devoid of ethics”. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif had raised the issue earlier, when he addressed the UN General Assembly last week. He did not mince his words when he said that diverting Pakistan’s water wouldamount to an “act of war”. This is not mere rhetoric. The Indus and its tributaries are Pakistan’s lifeline, and the country cannot allow India to blackmail it using these precious waters. India has ruled out restoring the treaty until Pakistan acts against ‘cross-border terrorism’. This is a weak alibi being deployed to take what belongs to Pakistan. New Delhi has remained adamant despite therulingby the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague in August that the IWT could not be unilaterally suspended. India has brushed aside the court’s decision. Along with the key issue of water rights, the larger question is what sort of precedent India wants to set. Its leaders speak of multilateralism and the global ‘rules-based order’. Yet in practice, when they scupper bilateral treaties and refuse to recognise decisions by respected arbitrators, the Indians in fact promote the law of the jungle. Pakistan must continue to pursue its legitimate rights with regard to the Indus waters. It must also point out the double standards India adheres to — claiming to uphold global norms, yet trampling on international law. If the IWT dispute is left to fester, or worse, if India takes further steps to cut off Pakistan’s share of water, a new conflict in South Asia is quite possible. In order to avoid such a grim scenario, saner elements in India must work towards restoring the IWT, and addressing all other outstanding issues in a civilised manner.
articles.author: Editorial
